title: Variables, identifiers, data types and constants

visuals.title: Match each term to its meaning

pairs.meaning: A named box in memory that stores a value
The name you choose for a variable or function
Tells what kind of value the box can hold
Giving a variable its first value
Makes a value that can never be changed
Tells how many bytes a type or variable uses

stages.name: Declare
stages.detail: Choose a type and a name: int marks; The computer reserves a box.

stages.name: Initialise
stages.detail: Put the first value in the box: marks = 85;

stages.name: Use
stages.detail: Read the value, for example print it with cout << marks;

stages.name: Change
stages.detail: Store a new value: marks = 90; The old value is replaced.

goal: After this you can declare and initialise variables of the basic types, choose valid names, use const, and check sizes with sizeof.
warmup: Think of the steel boxes (dabbay) in a canteen. One box has a label 'Samosa' and holds 5 pieces. Another is labelled 'Price' and holds 30 rupees. You can open a box, look inside, or replace what is in it. A variable is exactly this: a labelled box in the computer's memory. The label is the name, and what you put inside is the value.
definition: A variable is a named place in memory that stores a value, and the value can change. Every variable has a data type, which says what kind of value it can hold (whole number, decimal number, one character, true or false, or text). The name you give it is called an identifier. A constant is like a variable, but its value can never change after you set it.
howItWorks: Press Play and watch the Visualize tab. Each variable appears as a labelled box showing its type and value. Declaring a variable makes a new box. An assignment puts a value into the box. Reading a variable does not change it, but a new assignment replaces the old value. Remember: you must declare a variable (type + name) before you use it.

variations.when: Whole numbers (no decimal point), usually 4 bytes
Decimal numbers, about 7 digits of precision, 4 bytes
Decimal numbers, about 15 digits of precision, 8 bytes (the usual choice)
A single character in single quotes, 1 byte
true or false only (prints as 1 or 0)
Declare several variables of the same type in one line
A value that must never change
Find the size in bytes of a type or variable

mistakes.error: expected unqualified-id before numeric constant (a name cannot start with a digit)
'y' was not declared in this scope

mistakes.right:
const int MAX = 10;
// do not change MAX

mistakes.error: invalid conversion from 'const char*' to 'char' (use single quotes for one character)
expected initializer before 'marks' (names cannot contain spaces)

examTips: Identifier rules: letters, digits and underscore only; cannot start with a digit; no spaces; cannot be a keyword like int or return.
C++ is case-sensitive: marks, Marks and MARKS are three different variables.
Single quotes are for one char ('A'). Double quotes are for strings ("Ali").
int drops the decimal part: int n = 3.7; stores 3. Use double when you need decimals.
Know the sizes: char 1 byte, int 4, float 4, double 8. Declaration makes the box; initialisation fills it the first time.
romanSummary: Variable memory mein ek naam wali jagah hai jis mein value store hoti hai, aur value badal sakti hai.
Data types: int (poore number), float/double (decimal), char (ek character), bool (true/false), string (text).
Variable ka naam (identifier) digit se shuru nahi ho sakta, us mein space nahi hoti aur wo keyword nahi ho sakta.
const wali value ek baar set hone ke baad kabhi change nahi hoti.
sizeof batata hai ke koi type kitne bytes leta hai, jaise int 4 bytes.

practice.prompt: Which one is a valid variable name in C++?
practice.hint: Names cannot start with a digit, contain spaces, or be keywords.
practice.explanation: total_marks uses only letters and an underscore and is not a keyword.

practice.prompt:
Fill in the blank so the variable can store a decimal number:

______ price = 99.5;
practice.hint: It is the usual type for decimal numbers.
practice.explanation: double stores decimal numbers. (float also works, but double is the normal choice.)

practice.hint: x is changed before it is printed.
practice.explanation: x starts as 10. The assignment stores 10 + 5 = 15 in x, so 15 is printed.

practice.hint: A constant cannot be assigned again.
practice.explanation: const values cannot change. Remove the assignment (or make MAX a normal int if it must change).

practice.prompt:
What does this print on a normal computer?

cout << sizeof(char) + sizeof(int);
practice.hint: char is 1 byte and int is 4 bytes.

practice.prompt:
Fill in the blank so DAYS can never be changed:

______ int DAYS = 7;
practice.hint: It is the keyword for constants.
practice.explanation: const makes the value read-only after it is set.

practice.prompt: Write a program that stores a book's title (string), pages (int) and price (double) and prints all three on separate lines.
practice.hint: Use string, int and double, then three cout lines.
practice.explanation: Each value uses the type that fits it. #include <string> is needed for string.

practice.hint: An int cannot keep the decimal part.
practice.explanation: Storing 3.7 in an int drops the decimal part and keeps 3. d is unchanged, so it still prints 3.7.

options: A named place in memory that stores a value
quiz.answer: A named place in memory that stores a value
quiz.explanation: A variable is a named memory location. Its value can change.

quiz.prompt: Which data type stores a single character such as 'A'?
quiz.explanation: char holds one character, written in single quotes.

quiz.prompt: Which declaration is correct for the text "Ali"?
quiz.hint: Text needs the string type and double quotes.
quiz.explanation: A string holds text in double quotes. char holds only one character.

quiz.prompt: What happens if you try to change a const variable?
quiz.explanation: Assigning to a const variable is a compile error.

quiz.prompt: What is stored in int n = 9.8; ?
quiz.explanation: The decimal part is cut off (truncated), so n holds 9.
